The compound has been characterized as a hepatotoxic agent, consistent with hepatic bioactivation of reactive intermediates.
The compound has been identified as a hepatotoxic agent, and liver injury represents a principal target organ effect observed in experimental animal studies.

It is also employed as a deodorant and, historically, as an insecticide and soil fumigant, although its pesticide registrations in the United States have been cancelled and no currently registered pesticide products contain this substance.
Industrial products incorporating 1,2-dichlorobenzene include metal degreasing formulations and paint solvent preparations.

Human exposure may occur in occupational settings among chemical manufacturing plant operators, metal degreasing workers, paint formulators, and laboratory personnel through inhalation of vapors and dermal contact with the liquid.

Environmental exposure pathways include volatilization from industrial waste streams into ambient air, leaching from contaminated soil into groundwater, and adsorption to sediments in surface water bodies receiving industrial effluents.

1,2-Dichlorobenzene can be absorbed into the body by inhalation, through the skin, and by ingestion.
Inhalation represents the primary route of occupational exposure, given the compound's vapor pressure of 1.4 mm Hg at 25 °C, which supports meaningful volatilization under ambient conditions.

Following absorption, the compound is distributed to tissues throughout the body; consistent with its lipophilic character, distribution to adipose tissue and highly perfused organs, including the liver and kidneys, is anticipated.

ects of 1,2-dichlorobenzene in humans and experimental animals include irritation of the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract following inhalation or dermal contact, as well as central nervous system depression at high exposure concentrations.

rstood to involve cytochrome P450-mediated bioactivation to reactive arene oxide intermediates, which may covalently bind to cellular macromolecules, including proteins and DNA, thereby initiating cytotoxic and potentially genotoxic events.

Oxidative stress resulting from the generation of reactive oxygen species during metabolic activation is considered a contributing mechanism, particularly in the liver, where bioactivation is most active.
The phenolic and catechol metabolites produced during oxidative metabolism may undergo further redox cycling, amplifying oxidative damage to hepatic and renal tissues.
Glutathione depletion has been proposed as a secondary mechanism by which reactive intermediates overwhelm cellular antioxidant defenses, leading to lipid peroxidation and cell death.

No authoritative cancer classification has been identified from EPA, IARC, or other bodies, leaving the carcinogenic potential of 1,2-dichlorobenzene uncharacterized and preventing a weight-of-evidence determination.

dy, health-based oral exposure limits and drinking water guidelines cannot be derived from first principles, and benchmark dose modeling or read-across from structurally related dichlorobenzene isomers may be required as interim approaches.

the domain of risk characterization, no drinking water MCL or MCLG has been identified for 1,2-dichlorobenzene, meaning that environmental contamination of drinking water sources cannot be evaluated against an enforceable federal standard.
